opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a real tension. Every question you add costs you something: people get tired, some drop out, and the ones who stay may answer more carelessly toward the end. So there's a pull toward asking each thing once, cleanly.

But one of the most important things we've learned from these surveys is that the answers depend a lot on how you ask. If you ask "in what year will there be a 50% chance of this?" versus "what's the probability of this by a given year?", people give systematically different answers. The fixed-years framing tends to produce later-looking timelines than the fixed-probabilities framing. Similarly, asking about AI that can do every *task* better than humans versus AI that has automated every *occupation* gets wildly different answers, even though logically those should be pretty close, since if machines can do every task, they could presumably do every job.

So if we'd only asked one way, we'd have given people a single number that looked authoritative but was partly an artifact of the wording. Asking several ways makes the uncertainty visible. It tells you these aren't stable, carefully worked-out beliefs. They're quick judgments about a very hard question, and they're sensitive to framing, the way most human judgments are.

To manage the cost, we randomize. Not everyone gets every variant. Different respondents get different framings, so we can compare across groups without making the survey enormous for any one person. That also helps with order effects, since seeing one version can anchor how you answer the next.

I'd defend the redundancy as one of the more valuable parts of the project. It's less about getting the "right" number and more about honestly showing the shape of expert opinion, including where it's incoherent. That incoherence is itself important information for anyone trying to lean on these forecasts.

r001.rationale: It says answers depend substantially on wording and gives examples of similar forecast questions producing systematically different timelines.

r002.rationale: It discusses wording artifacts and survey burden, but does not say that asking multiple ways lets someone selectively publicize a preferred answer.

r003.rationale: It does not describe people expecting near-term AI discounting full labor-automation forecasts as implausibly distant.

r004.rationale: It notes that one framing yields later timelines, but does not state that the answers together strongly counter the narrative that AI is arriving soon.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we did fairly deliberately in the surveys, and I think it's been one of the more interesting findings to come out of them, honestly. The basic setup is that we ask about the same underlying thing, something like when high-level machine intelligence arrives, but we frame it differently for different subsets of respondents. So some people get asked, "By what year do you think there's a fifty percent chance?" and others get asked, "What's the probability this happens by 2040?" or by some fixed year. And in principle those should give you the same distribution if people have a coherent picture in their heads.

What we actually find is that they don't. The framing shifts the answers a lot, sometimes by decades in terms of the implied median. If you ask people for the probability of something by a given year, they tend to give you answers implying earlier timelines than if you ask them which year hits a given probability. That's a pretty large effect, and it's been robust across the years we've run the survey.

So on the tradeoff question. The cost is obvious: you're using up respondent attention, and you can't ask everyone everything, so each individual question gets a smaller sample. And you end up with results that are harder to summarize. People want a single number, "AI researchers think AGI arrives in year X," and instead you have to say, well, it depends how you ask, here are two or three numbers and they disagree.

But I think the benefit clearly outweighs that, because the alternative is that you pick one framing, report one number, and present a false precision about what researchers believe. The disagreement between framings is itself the finding. It tells you that the experts don't have stable, well-formed beliefs about this, and that the number you'd have reported from a single framing is partly an artifact of how you worded the question. If you'd only asked one way, you'd never know that, and you'd be more confident than you should be.

There's also a more practical point, which is that once you know the framing effects exist, you can at least try to be honest about the range rather than reporting the one that happens to sound dramatic or happens to sound reassuring. I think a lot of the public discussion of these surveys cites the one number that fits whatever point the person is making, and having multiple framings makes that harder to do without someone noticing.

So I guess my overall take is that it's less a tradeoff between accuracy and simplicity, and more that the simplicity was never really available. The messiness was always there, and asking multiple ways just makes it visible instead of hiding it inside one question wording.

r001.rationale: It says differently framed versions of the same forecast produce substantially different answers, sometimes implying timelines decades apart, and identifies this as a framing effect.

r002.rationale: It notes that public discussion can cite whichever single number supports a preferred point, and that multiple framings make this selective presentation easier to spot.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention expectations that AI will arrive soon, forecasts of full labor automation, or discounting those forecasts as implausibly distant.

r004.rationale: The response does not say that the combined survey answers counter the narrative that AI is arriving soon.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a tradeoff between getting more information and using up people’s time and attention. If you ask questions that seem very similar, that can be frustrating, especially in a survey that’s already quite long. But it’s useful to know how much the answers depend on exactly how you ask.

For instance, asking what probability someone assigns to AI reaching some milestone by a particular year isn’t necessarily going to give you the same answer as asking what year they think it has a fifty percent chance of reaching that milestone—even though those answers should fit together. People don’t necessarily have a fully worked-out probability distribution in their heads that they’re just reporting.

So I think asking in different ways is valuable as a check on how we should interpret the forecasts. If the answers change a lot with the framing, that’s something we want to know. But you can often do that by giving different versions to different respondents, rather than making every person answer all of them.

r001.rationale: The response says similar questions can yield different answers and that changes with framing are useful to identify.

r002.rationale: It discusses comparing question formats but does not mention selectively publicizing a preferred answer.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss people expecting AI soon or discounting forecasts about full labor automation.

r004.rationale: It does not characterize the combined survey answers as a counter-signal to the narrative that AI is arriving soon.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a tradeoff between getting more information about what people believe and using up their time and attention. If you ask what sounds like the same question several times, that can be frustrating, and you might prefer to use that space to ask about something else.

But with these forecasting questions, it’s often unclear how much the answer depends on the wording. Asking for the probability of AI arriving by a particular year can produce a different picture from asking for the year by which there’s a particular probability. Those are, in principle, ways of eliciting the same belief, but people don’t necessarily answer them consistently.

So I think there’s quite a lot of value in asking in multiple ways, at least to understand how robust the results are. If the answers differ substantially, that’s something we want to know before putting too much weight on any one forecast.

r001.rationale: The response says seemingly equivalent forecasts can produce different answers depending on wording, and that substantial differences reveal a lack of robustness—communicating framing effects.

r002.rationale: It discusses the cost of asking questions in multiple ways, but does not say this lets people selectively publicize a preferred answer.

r003.rationale: It does not mention expectations of AI arriving soon or discounting forecasts of full labor automation as implausibly distant.

r004.rationale: It does not say the survey answers together counter the narrative that AI is arriving soon.
